sections.title: Get your data from a test you already had
sections.summary: If you or your child already had a clinical genetic test (a gene panel, exome or genome), the lab usually still holds the data files behind the report. The labs below describe how to ask for them. Usually your doctor sends the request, or you sign the lab's consent form. Expect a wait of several weeks, and possibly a fee.

file_types.plain: A list of the places where your DNA differs from the standard reference. Small, around 2 MB for an exome.

quotes: VCF (Variant Call Format) is a standard file format storing a list of sequence variants and their genomic positions.
It is ~2 MB in size.

file_types.plain: The sequencing reads lined up against the reference genome. Large, about 4-8 GB for an exome.

quotes: BAM (Binary sequence Alignment Map) is a standard file format that contains sequence reads mapped to the human reference genome, including base quality and mapping quality scores.
BAM files are ~4-8 GB in size.

file_types.plain: The raw sequence reads straight off the machine, before alignment.

quotes: The FASTQ data files (text-based format for storing nucleotide sequences)

file_types.plain: A compressed alternative to BAM. None of the lab pages checked here mention CRAM, so ask the lab whether it can supply it.

labs.who_can_ask: A healthcare provider, the patient, or a parent/guardian.
labs.how_to_request: Fill in Labcorp's 'Consent for release of genetic testing data' form, signed by each person whose data is requested and by a healthcare provider. Labcorp then contacts you with download details. Allow about 30 days.
labs.caveats: Labcorp says the files can contain unprocessed and unreported data, including false positives, and medical decisions should not be based on them without a genetics professional.
labs.invitae_note: Invitae's website now carries a Labcorp copyright line. This form is a Labcorp form; ask Labcorp Genetic Services whether it applies to an older Invitae test.

quotes: A healthcare provider, patient, or parent/guardian can request the release of genetic testing data for a patient.
Signed consent is required from each individual for whom data is being requested.
Data will be provided via electronic file transfer. Please allow 30 days for requests to be fulfilled.
FASTQ (WES and WGS only)
I understand the data files may contain false positive and unconfirmed results.

rights.name: EU GDPR, Article 15: right of access
rights.plain: In the EU, you can ask an organisation that holds your personal data, such as a genetic testing lab, to confirm it holds the data and to give you a copy. If you ask electronically, the copy normally comes in a common electronic format.

quotes: The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller confirmation as to whether or not personal data concerning him or her are being processed, and, where that is the case, access to the personal data
The controller shall provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing.
Where the data subject makes the request by electronic means, and unless otherwise requested by the data subject, the information shall be provided in a commonly used electronic form.

rights.name: UK GDPR, Article 15: right of access (subject access request)
rights.plain: The UK has the same right of access, called a subject access request (SAR). The ICO says organisations usually have one month to respond.

quotes: The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller confirmation as to whether or not personal data concerning him or her are being processed, and, where that is the case, access to the personal data
The controller shall provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing
You can also ask them for copies of your personal information.
Organisations usually have one month to respond to a SAR.

rights.name: US HIPAA Privacy Rule: right of access (45 CFR 164.524)
rights.plain: In the US, HIPAA gives you the right to inspect and get a copy of your health information held in a 'designated record set'. HHS guidance says that for a lab covered by HIPAA this includes your lab test reports and the underlying data. For next generation sequencing, it includes the full gene variant information. Covered entities must act within 30 calendar days, with one possible 30-day extension.

quotes: an individual has a right of access to inspect and obtain a copy of protected health information about the individual in a designated record set
source.source_note: Text fetched from the eCFR renderer API (https://www.ecfr.gov/api/renderer/v1/content/enhanced/current/title-45?part=164&section=164.524).

quotes: The designated record set includes not only the laboratory test reports but also the underlying information generated as part of the test, as well as other information concerning tests a laboratory runs on an individual.

a clinical laboratory that is a HIPAA covered entity and that conducts next generation sequencing (NGS) of DNA on an individual must provide the individual, upon the individual’s request for PHI concerning the NGS, with a copy of the completed test report, the full gene variant information generated by the test, as well as any other information in the designated record set concerning the test.

request_letter_template.label: General information, not legal advice
request_letter_template.title: Request for a copy of my genetic test data
request_letter_template.how_to_use: Edit the [brackets], delete the lines that don't apply, and send it to the lab's records, privacy or client services contact, or ask your doctor to send it. Many labs have their own form (see the lab list above). If they do, use their form, and you can attach this letter.
request_letter_template.body:
[Your name]
[Your address]
[Email / phone]
[Date]

To: [Laboratory name], [Records / Privacy / Client Services team]

Subject: Request for a copy of genetic test data for [patient name], date of birth [DD/MM/YYYY]

Dear [Laboratory name] team,

I am writing to request a copy of the personal health information you hold about [me / my child, for whom I am the parent or legal guardian], relating to the following genetic test:
- Test name: [e.g. exome sequencing / gene panel]
- Lab reference or accession number: [number, if known]
- Ordering clinician: [name, hospital]
- Approximate date of sample: [month / year]

Please provide:
1. The final test report(s).
2. Where available, the underlying data files generated by the test, such as [VCF] [BAM or CRAM] [FASTQ].

[US: I make this request under my right of access in the HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 CFR 164.524).]
[EU/UK: I make this request under my right of access in Article 15 of the GDPR / UK GDPR.]

I would prefer to receive the files electronically, by [secure download link / other method]. If you need a specific form, proof of identity, proof of guardianship or a signature from my doctor, please tell me what is required. If there is a fee, please tell me the amount before you process the request.

I understand that raw data files can contain unconfirmed or unreported findings, and that I should discuss any questions about them with a doctor or genetic counsellor.

Thank you,
[Signature]
[Printed name]
[Relationship to patient, if not the patient]

sections.title: If you haven't had genetic testing
sections.summary: There are three main routes: through a doctor or genetic counsellor, through a sponsored no-cost testing programme, or through a research study. Most need a doctor's involvement. Sponsored programmes are paid for by companies or charities, and the companies may receive de-identified data.

route_types.doctor_or_counsellor: Through a doctor or genetic counsellor

routes.name: NSGC 'Find a Genetic Counselor' directory
routes.referral_note: Anyone can search the directory, in person or by telehealth. NSGC says it is not a referral service. Check your insurance coverage.
routes.eligibility_in_source_words: The Find a Genetic Counselor directory offers access to over 3,300 genetic counselors (US and Canada).

quotes: The Find a Genetic Counselor directory offers access to over 3,300 genetic counselors (US and Canada).
The NSGC Find A Counselor directory is not a referral service but rather a service to provide an up-to-date list of NSGC members.
Searches of the “Via Telehealth” directory will show genetic counselors who meet with patients via phone, video conferencing and other virtual methods.
Check with your insurance company to verify coverage of genetic counseling, testing and authorized providers.

routes.name: Genetic and genomic testing on the NHS
routes.referral_note: A doctor must refer you. Testing is free on the NHS when a hospital specialist refers you. You may also be referred to a genetic counsellor.
routes.eligibility_in_source_words: You will generally only be referred if you have a suspected genetic health condition or if you have a particular type of cancer.

quotes: You need to be referred for genetic testing by a doctor.
Genetic testing is free on the NHS if you are referred for it by a hospital specialist.
You will generally only be referred if you have a suspected genetic health condition or if you have a particular type of cancer.
If you're offered a genetic test, you may be referred to a genetic counsellor to help you think through what the test means for you and your family.

sections.title: Consumer tests: what they can and can't tell you
sections.summary: Many consumer DNA tests use a genotyping array (a 'SNP chip'). It checks a preset list of DNA positions and does not read your genes in full the way clinical sequencing does. Arrays work well for common variants but are unreliable for very rare variants, which usually cause single-gene (rare) conditions. A rare-disease result in consumer raw data can be a false alarm, and a clear result does not rule a condition out. Any finding needs confirming with a clinical test ordered through a doctor or genetic counsellor.
sections.not_recommendations: This atlas does not list or recommend consumer DNA companies.

points.plain: Consumer chips are good at common variants, but most of their 'positive' calls for very rare variants are wrong.

quotes: SNP chips are extremely unreliable for genotyping very rare pathogenic variants and should not be used to guide health decisions without validation.
Single gene disorders are usually caused by genetic variants that are very rare in the population (<1 in 10 000 people).
only 16% of 4757 heterozygous genotypes from the SNP chips were confirmed with sequencing data
many SNP chip designs, including those used by many direct to consumer companies, have been augmented to include rare pathogenic variants that cause single gene disorders
source.source_note: Weedon MN et al. Use of SNP chips to detect rare pathogenic variants: retrospective, population based diagnostic evaluation. BMJ 2021;372:n214. PMID 33589468.

points.plain: Downloaded consumer raw data contains thousands of extra rare variants that have not been quality-checked.

quotes: which will often include many thousands of additional rare variants assayed on their SNP chip that have not undergone stringent quality control and are therefore much more likely to be false positives

points.plain: When a clinical lab re-tested variants that people found in their consumer raw data, 40% turned out to be false positives.

quotes: Our analyses indicated that 40% of variants in a variety of genes reported in DTC raw data were false positives.
source.source_note: Tandy-Connor S et al. False-positive results released by direct-to-consumer genetic tests highlight the importance of clinical confirmation testing for appropriate patient care. Genet Med 2018;20(12):1515-1521.

points.plain: A negative consumer result doesn't rule a condition out, because these tests don't look at every variant. The FDA says they are not a substitute for seeing a healthcare provider.

quotes: Some genetic health risk tests do not report all known genetic variants that might contribute to an increased risk of disease.
Remember that direct-to-consumer tests are not a substitute for a traditional health care evaluation, including health screenings and visits to your health care provider.
For genetic tests, you may also consider speaking with a genetic counselor, board-certified medical geneticist, or other equivalent health care provider.
